children: Wall Street rallied on Friday after the latest consumer inflation report came in broadly in line with expectations, helping ease concerns over price pressures and supporting a rebound across risk assets.
On Friday, the Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 0.9%, while the S&P 500 (
) advanced 0.86%, and the Nasdaq Composite climbed 0.9%.
Despite Friday’s rebound, the S&P 500 slipped 0.8% for the week.
Seeking Alpha analyst

noted, “The week was dominated by macroeconomic factors, particularly oil, which once again surpassed $100, and bond yields, which continued to be a nuisance. After three negative sessions, stock indices closed the week with a strange surge higher, despite the still-high inflation figure, which increased the probability of a rate hike at the September meeting from 60% to 90%. After the figure, yields first rose, then fell. Equities initially moved lower, then recovered and closed the day in the green. This was most likely because investors decided to look through the bad news already priced in, such as the September rate hike, while still discounting the possibility of a new round of Fed tightening.”
From a sector-level perspective, three S&P sectors ended the week in positive territory, while the remaining eight sectors finished in the red.
Energy
and Communication Services
were the strongest-performing sectors of the week, gaining 1.7% and 0.54%, respectively.
Seeking Alpha analyst

highlighted that it's no surprise to see energy up again this week after the recent gains in oil. The longer and messier the U.S.-Iran war gets, the more I expect we'll see energy gain, as their revenues will stay higher for longer. Megacap tech firms (GOOGL, MSFT, etc.) held their ground, which buoyed both tech and communications in a week where there was otherwise a lot of market pain.
Conversely, Health Care
and Materials
posted the weakest weekly performances, falling 3.52% and 2.84%, respectively.

Bowman concluded, “When defensive sectors like healthcare and cyclical sectors like industrials sell off together, it tends to tell me that we're looking at rate fears plaguing the market. When a macro thesis is driving, there isn't much room for traditional defense, and I expect that volatility to continue across both defensives and cyclicals until we get clarity on rates next week.”
